question.problem:
For $\mathbf x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z\in\mathbb R^2,$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)))$ evaluated at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/7625625edbb65c637775812baec802a512b580b45e94c896764377cd23a0f946.svg)
question.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{C}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} = \mathbf{C}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{z}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/aa560155df00efd7959768d56e38ef7fea999b06d2bfe5515b1af01f2184aaf4.svg)
Evaluating at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/9ee03503efd8d3da6a4aa7e012eef1d0e390d014aa6ceae1b0f18acd82b5c08f.svg) we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/73522ffceb4c0e0f4d3cad330414660ad822609c67a0a0024cdab2cb62c13778.svg)

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 7 \\ 3 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
